title: Not Misusing Sex
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the precept on not misusing sex, opening with Allen Ginsberg's poem "Song" and its line "The weight of the world is love." Nomon traces the Buddha's monastic rules, where sexual intercourse is the first offense bringing permanent expulsion, then names the destructive side of sexual power through wartime rape, including the Bosnian rape camps. Nomon turns to Robert Aitken's Mind of Clover, which finds only one koan on sexuality, and reads the old woman who burns the hermitage of a monk "a withered tree on a cold boulder," and Miao Zong's interview with the monk Wanan. Nomon closes by rereading the Ginsberg poem and inviting a conversation the next Wednesday at six.

sentences.text: I was appreciating, when I came back into the zendo, just that feeling of everyone's efforts to be steady, to take up this practice as best we can.
I was really reflecting, it's not easy, actually.
At first, it seems like maybe it would be a physically demanding thing to sit a particular way, sit really still.
Sometimes it does seem physically demanding, especially at the beginning, maybe in the middle and the end too.
But I don't think that's really what's difficult.
I think what's difficult is just actually really showing up for our own life in a sustained, steady way and being willing to feel what we're feeling.
We have so many ways that we're a little bit resistant to our life just the way it is.
We want a little bit of improvement, a little bit different.
Some other version of me would be nice.
This practice really calls on us to just be with ourselves just the way we are, and that's pretty hard.
Thank you for that effort and such a feeling of mutual support.
If things are working well, then the others around us support us in doing that effort.

I was really appreciating the chanting because in the chanting what I was having fun doing was listening to the different voices, picking out the different voices, and I could hear the voices of people.

I've been lucky enough to chant with for 20 years and more, and 10 years and 2 years, and for the first time tonight, all are so wonderful, all the different voices and yet somehow coming together, one voice.
I was just appreciating our practice, that sometimes it seems like maybe the talk is going to give us some new information, something outside of just the actual doing the practice, some new ideas.
Especially tonight our topic is sex, so we hope for some light on this dark and difficult topic.

Whether or not that will happen, I don't know, but what we do know is that we are and have been in a really beautiful way bringing forward something important, something simple, something ordinary and something really important about what it is to be a human being, which may prove to be the most important ingredient for our sexual lives to be healthy also.

Another sort of pre-announcement: if you were here, you remember that one of the interesting things about this school of Buddhism is that the precepts we're talking about, we're having a series of talks about precepts for ethical living from the Zen tradition.

The precepts in this tradition are not just guidelines for ethical living; they have also taken on a kind of a power of support and sort of spiritual depth and growth that studying them and agreeing to them and receiving them in some way into our heart has a sort of power in this tradition.
We have a ceremony where people formally receive these precepts.
They also receive this little bib-like thing that some people are wearing called rakusu, which we think was invented in China about the eighth century when there were terrible Buddhist repressions.
It was a way for the Buddhist clergy who had to defrock just secretly, they'd wear that under their clothes, we think.

We don't really know for sure the origins of the rakusu, but that's the best theory, that it's like a covert way of being a priest because originally these precepts as empowerment were only received by priests.
Another innovation of our particular line of Zen, Soto Zen, is to provide a way for them to be available to people who are not priests who can receive these precepts.

I just want to mention that seven people in our community are going to start doing the hand sewing practice work of creating that garment for themselves that they'll receive in the ceremony, which is kind of great in a way, too.
You create it, you give it away, and you receive it again.

I live in fear that I'll forget a name, but the seven people are Jeffrey Harker, who lives now in Sammamish but practices with us regularly; Suzanne Nguyen, who started practicing with us years ago and moved away to her husband's job, had two kids—there's a whole different person now, a mid-30s mother of two instead of a 20-something exploring young woman—so that's wonderful that she'll receive the precepts here; Dave Lynch, who is here; Kevin Connor; Georgia Mitchell; two more, should have written it down; Bob Rose, who lives in Anacortes but has been coming regularly; and the seventh person will come to me in a moment, Jeff McKenna.
The ceremony has a lot of elements, so we'll talk more about it another time.
One of the primary elements is it's kind of a sense of entering a family; it's a family entering ceremony.
The Japanese title for the ceremony is Zaikei Tokudo.
Jukai is another word that's used; Jukai means to receive the precepts.
Zaikei Tokudo means staying at home and receiving the way.
Staying at home and receiving the way.
That's what they're going to do.
We're going to start this Saturday, and it will be a slow process, which many of them have been involved in already for many months or years.
Hopefully in October we'll have a ceremony.
I want to mention that these precepts have so many dimensions.

Allen Ginsberg wrote a poem called Song in 1956 as a young man, and it's about our deepest problem, which seems to be this feeling of separation, isolation, being alone, which itself has so many elements: fear, unworthiness, doubt.
So it's a primal kind of problem.
Here's a poem from Allen Ginsberg about this question of separation:
*The weight of the world is love.
Under the burden of solitude, under the burden of dissatisfaction, the weight, the weight we carry is love.
Who can deny in dreams it touches the body?
Thought constructs a miracle in imagination, anguishes till born inhuman, looks out of the heart, turning with purity for the burden of life is love.
But we carry the weight warily and we must rest in the arms of love.
At last must rest in the arms of love.
No rest without love, no sleep without dreams of love.
Be mad or chill, obsessed with angels or machines.
The frail wish is love, cannot be bitter, cannot deny, cannot withhold if denied.
The weight is too heavy.
Must give for no return as thought is given.
In solitude, in all the excellence of its excess, the warm bodies shine together in the darkness.
The hand moves to the center of the flesh.
The skin trembles in happiness and the soul comes joyful to the eye.
Yes, yes, that's what I wanted.*
I always wanted, I always wanted to return to the body where I was born.
One of the powers that only gods have is the power to create life.
It's a very magical and mysterious power.
Yet two human beings can create life being as gods, and so sexuality has that power, has that weight.
A strong power and a strong weight can turn in many different directions with incredible energy and incredible violence and incredible love.
The Buddha when he created the monastic order didn't want to deal with this; it was like too hard, too powerful.

Following, and partly he was following the usual plan for serious religious practitioners of his day, the emerging groups of wandering shramana—shaman, same root as shaman—they had shramanas, shramanas were wandering religious people, mostly men probably, a little different from the Brahmanical sort of mainstream order.
They were all celibate.

The Buddha had his monks and nuns; once he invited nuns to join the celibate, and when the monastic rules were created, remembering that our sixteen precepts are in a way a reinvention of these monastic rules, there are only four rules which merit expulsion from the order, permanent expulsion from the order, no return.
The very first rule is sexual intercourse; that's the first parajika rule where you are barred for life, although oral sex is a slightly lesser one.
But it's up there with stealing and killing somebody or condoning the death of somebody.
Interestingly, the fourth parajika offense for which you are expelled from the order is lying about your mental state.
Lying about your mental state, especially in the service of bragging about your spiritual attainment.
But the way it's translated literally here is lying about your mental state.
Boy, we do that all the time.
So that's something to think about.
Someone asks us, "How are you?"
You're in danger; you can be honest.
There are thirteen sangadhisesa, sangadhisesa precepts, which are like suspension from the order.
You have to confess; you have to do like a penance, very much like other systems.
You have to be repentant.
These five of those thirteen are sexual.
I won't list them all; I have a nice little handout I can send it to you on PDF or put it on the website.
I made a little handout of what the original rules were for the monks: twenty-two seven precepts for the monks, another thirty or forty for the nuns.
Six of the first nine are about sex.
So this is a serious thing, very powerful.
Of course, that great power of gods can be turned in a horrible way, too, a really horrible way.
Forty-four percent of victims of sexual assault are under eighteen.
Every two minutes, someone in the U.S. is sexually assaulted.
Fifty-four percent of those sexual assaults are never reported to the police.
Ninety-seven percent of people who commit sexual crimes think they are never punished by the legal system.
It gets even worse during wartime; sexuality, rape, used as a weapon.
This became mostly to the public eye during the Bosnian conflict.
It got so bad that they had to include mass rape as a crime against humanity; that's when that was invented.
There's a really horrible article in Wikipedia about rape in war; it's eleven pages long, and it goes way back.

I won't depress too many statistics, but just a few highlights for us to bear witness to this incredibly destructive power that is, of course, a perversion of sex, and yet has an element from that power to give and create life turned on its head, turned into killing life, turned into destruction.
The Japanese army, when it was controlling a good section of China, created a system of brothels for the soldiers.
As many as two hundred thousand women were pressed into service as prostitutes.
Our own American army is not exempt from this shameful history.

After the U.S. successfully took back the southernmost island of Japan, Okinawa, quite a bit south of the main part of Japan, but it's part of mainland Japan, U.S. soldiers raped as many as one thousand three hundred Okinawan women during the first ten days of the occupation.

There's equally horrible stuff about the German army when they invaded the Soviet Union, and then right back the other way at the end of the war, the Soviet Union on the side of the victors occupying what became eastern Germany, thousands of documented rapes, and probably many thousands more than that.
And back to Bosnia.
Serbo-Croatian society is patriarchal, so your ethnicity is judged to be the ethnicity of your father.
Now, if we were standing in front of a Croatian person and a Serbian person, I don't know if we'd be able to tell them apart, but they could certainly tell each other apart.
The Serbian army created rape camps with the intent of impregnating women so that the children born would be Serbian.
At least thirty-five thousand women are documented to have been held in these rape camps and raped, probably many more.
Maybe just a moment of silence for all that.
Sexual energy is interesting too, isn't it?
Because when it's here and we're aware of it, so strong, right?
So strong, it changes the way we think, changes our emotions, changes our body.
Other times it's not so apparent.
I was remembering the last time we did a thorough kind of working through the precepts.
Nancy and I co-led a class some years ago, and we got to this precept on sex, and it wasn't really up for me.
It wasn't, I guess, really up for Nancy.
We just kind of said, oh, well, you know, you all know about this one, not a big one.
Which is funny to say, but it has that quality too, doesn't it?
It sort of slips under the radar in a certain way.
We can also forget that we are sexual beings and forget about the power of that energy, which is maybe why it surprises us with such ferocity at times when it emerges, because we've forgotten.

Robert Aitken's chapter on this precept, as we're, as a sangha, trying to read or reread this book, *Mind of Clover*, which is just re-impressing me anew, talks about talks given by Robert Aitken, an American Zen teacher in the 1970s.
But his chapter on sex is probably his weakest chapter, and you can see if you agree with me or not, if you read it or are going to read it.
He seems to have been not terribly in touch with the power and the depth of sexuality when he gave that talk.
One of the things he mentions is that the treasure trove of knowledge in the Zen tradition is in the stories.
So we have all kinds of teachings and scriptures and so on, but the real treasure trove is in the stories, the Zen koan stories.
He mentions in there that he had a big index of koans, and he could only find one that had anything at all to do with sexuality.
He's lamenting that the Zen school is ignorant on this topic; they hadn't tried to work with it.

I'll read you that story and then mention a few others, because now we have the good fortune in our time and place that many of the stories that were lost or hidden weren't available to Robert Aitken in the 1970s, even though he could read Japanese and had access to all the texts that were available.
We have more stories about women and surrounding women, and so sexuality can be reintroduced and explored as a spiritual question, as a practice question, and as a very important question.
Here's a story that Robert Aitken did mention.
This, as well as the other two I'm going to mention, are in the forthcoming book, *The Hidden Transmission of the Lamp*, edited by a few colleagues of ours in the Bay Area.
An old woman in China supported a monk for many years.
She built him a hermitage and provided him with food and clothing.
After twenty years, she wondered what he had attained and resolved to test him.
She summoned a beautiful girl from the village and sent her to the hermit with instructions to embrace him and ask him how he felt.
The girl did that, went in, caressed the monk, and asked, "How do you feel just now?"
The monk said, "A withered tree on a cold boulder has no warmth in winter."
The woman returned to the old woman, the girl returned to the old woman, and told her what had happened.
What?
The old woman said, "To think I've been supporting that imposter for all these years."
She grabbed the stick, hurried to the hermitage, beat the monk, shouted, "Get out of here," and burned the hermitage to the ground.

It seemed the understanding of the old woman was not that it's about denial of our feelings, of our human feelings, including sexual feelings, so a mistake to repress or deny, even if you're a celibate monk.
Here's another story.
This is on that last story.
We don't know when in China that was supposed to have taken place, but this one was supposed to have taken place in China in the twelfth century.
It's called Miao Zong's Dharma Interview.
Before Miao Zong became a nun, she used to visit Master Da Hui's monastery and study with him.
He gave her a room in the abbot's quarters.
She was traveling from a ways away, so she had to spend the night.
I was just telling somebody you can spend the night here in the Dharma Hall, so we carry on that tradition.
The abbot gave her a room in his area, in his suite.
The senior monk, Wanan, did not approve of this, scandalous behavior.
Da Hui, the teacher, said to him, "Although she's a woman, she has outstanding merits."
Wanan, the head monk, still disapproved.
Da Hui urged him to have an interview with Miao Zong, the nun-to-be, since she was not yet ordained.
Wanan reluctantly agreed and requested an interview.
Miao Zong said, "Do you want a Dharma interview or a worldly interview?"
Wanan said, "A Dharma interview.
You don't want the whole thing."
Miao Zong said, "Then please send your attendants away."
She went into the room first, and after a few moments she called out, "Please come in."
When Wanan, the head monk, entered, he saw Miao Zong lying naked on her back on the bed.
He pointed at her genitals, saying, "What is this place?"
Miao Zong replied, "All the Buddhas of the three worlds, the six patriarch, and all great monks everywhere came out of this place."
Wanan asked, "May I enter?"
Miao Zong replied, "Horses may cross, asses may not."
Wanan was unable to reply.
Miao Zong declared, "I have met you, senior monk.
This interview is over."
She turned her back to him.
Wanan left ashamed.
Later at Dahui, the teacher said to Wanan, "The old dragon has some wisdom, doesn't she?
And I want to just tell you a little bit about the commentary."
These are a collection of one hundred stories, Zen stories, featuring and about and honoring women.
And then there are commentaries from one hundred women Dharma teachers, contemporary women Dharma teachers.
This is going to be a fantastic book when it comes out.
Tao has discussed some stories from this in his classes.
We have a pre-release version; we're really excited.
The commentary on this case in the book is by Chris Fortin.
I don't know if you've ever met Chris Fortin.
She's one of the priests in the Bay Area everyday Zen group ordained by Norman, a wonderful person.
I heard her talk about this before, and she describes it in here that she hosts an annual women's retreat.
You might think about going one year.
These stories were starting to come out, and so in the women's retreat, they decided to act out the story.
We performed a skit.
Here are Chris's words: "We performed a skit of this koan on the opening evening of the retreat.
I volunteered to be Miao Zong.
I wore a flesh-colored full-body stocking, and I was deeply moved and jolted by the experience of entering into Miao Zong's skin and enacting her fearlessness and compassionate activity.

Here was direct body-to-body, heart-to-heart transmission across time and space from a full-blooded woman who had no shame about her body and who was a deeply realized practitioner to me, a woman practitioner more than a thousand years later."
So there's something about these stories that can transmit something.
I have another story.
I'll put the other story on the website when I have time tonight.
Sex, of course, is very personal, very private, very emotional.
Each of us has our own journey through adolescence, being the father of a preadolescent kid.

We're really wondering about this right now at our house: how can we take our place, fully take our place as adults with this possibility of deeply touching another, fully touching another human being?
Whether we happen to be opposite gender or the same gender doesn't matter.
The body longs to be touched, and two bodies can become like one body, creating life in many dimensions.
So easily it goes astray, right?
So easily this power to give life and create wholeness and connection can create divisiveness and hurt, and people can spend a lifetime recovering from that hurt, or maybe more than one lifetime.
I don't know if I am in a position to give anybody any advice about this.
I get as confused as anybody.
But sometimes, sometimes we're in alignment with these powerful energies in the body, in the mind and in the heart, and nothing could be better.

Maybe that's why we're sitting Zazen, to see if we can feel our way into that kind of alignment and that kind of harmony that we can bring forward to our friendships, to our relationships, to our relationships that somehow, through some strange circumstances, the situation is right that we can have loving physical contact.
And like the old monk, we can't shy away from it either.
It's here.
It's a part of our humanity.
It's our responsibility to find out how to hold it wisely so that we can create life.
I'll close again with Alan Ginsberg.
I really look forward to a conversation with as many of you who have time next Wednesday at six about all this.
We can reflect on it, read.
I'll try to get the stuff on the website, and I hope to have a very honest and intimate conversation next week about this.
*The weight of the world is love.
Under the burden of solitude, under the burden of dissatisfaction, the weight, the weight we carry is love.

Who can deny in dreams it touches the body, in thought constructs a miracle, in imagination anguishes till born inhuman, looks out of the heart, burning with purity, burning with purity, for the burden of life is love.

But we carry the weight wearily, and so must rest in the arms of love at last, must rest in the arms of love, no rest without love, no sleep without dreams of love, be mad or chill, obsessed with angels or machines, the final wish is love.

Cannot be bitter, cannot deny, cannot withhold if denied, the weight is too heavy, must give for no return as though as thought is given in solitude, in all the excellence of its excess, the warm bodies shine together in the darkness, the hand moves to the center of the flesh, the skin trembles in happiness, and the soul comes joyful to the eye.
Yes, yes, that's what I wanted, I always wanted, I always wanted to return to the body where I was born.*
